prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map shows a top-down egocentric view looking down at a floor or large dog bed roughly 0.8 to 1.2 metres below the camera wearer, with a brown-and-white dog moving in the foreground within arm's reach at about 0.4 to 0.9 metres away. Across the five frames, the dog starts on the far right (partly out of view in frame 1), moves to the centre in frame 2 facing away with its head nearer the bottom edge and tail raised further away, shifts to the lower left in frame 3 as the wearer's right hand enters at the bottom right (about 0.5 metres away and 0.1 metres from the dog's snout), turns to face downward toward a small toy between the wearer's two hands in frame 4 (with its head brightest at roughly 0.4 metres), and turns away again in frame 5 with its head at the bottom edge. No other people are visible in the scene, and the camera wearer's own body is completely out of view except for the hands reaching in during frames 3 and 4. The depth map makes it easier than the motion-blurred RGB strip to see the vertical elevation of the dog's raised head, ears, and curved tail above the floor surface, as well as the continuous floor gradient sloping away toward the top of the frame. However, the depth map is unreliable in frame 4 where the wearer's extended left and right arms appear darker (falsely further away, around 0.8 to 1.0 metres) than the floor and the dog's head right beside them, and in frame 5 where the dog's rear blends smoothly into the floor depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map attempts to outline the foreground entities against the floor below the camera wearer, capturing the dog on the right in frame 1 (within 0.6 to 0.9 metres and partly clipped by the right edge) and tracking the main foreground regions across frames 2 to 5 within arm's reach (0.4 to 1.0 metres). While it provides a sharp silhouette of the dog's left leg and body on the right side of frame 1 that separates it from the motion-blurred carpet, the map is heavily unreliable in both class labels and spatial boundaries across the entire strip. Specifically, it mislabels the spotted dog as two 'giraffe' instances in frame 1, and in frames 2, 3, 4, and 5 it merges the dog, the surrounding dog bed/carpet, and the camera wearer's hands into giant single masks mislabelled as 'person' (frames 2 and 3), 'bear' (frame 4), and 'dog' (frame 5). Because the masks bleed across the floor and over the wearer's hands in frames 3 and 4, the segmentation map completely obscures the separation between the dog, the floor surface beneath it, the small object on the floor, and the wearer's reaching hands within 0.1 metres of the dog's head. It also fails to segment the crate or furniture pieces partially visible at the top-left and far-right edges of the scene roughly 1.0 to 1.5 metres away.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is entirely blank across frames 1, 2, 4, and 5, and detects only a single magenta right-hand skeleton for the camera wearer in the lower-right quadrant of frame 3. In frame 3, this detected right hand is positioned roughly 0.5 metres in front of and below the camera wearer, just to the right of the dog's head (within 0.1 to 0.2 metres of its snout) and within immediate arm's reach, with the fingers curled slightly inward toward the left side of the frame. No other people are present in the room, so no yellow body skeletons appear anywhere, and the camera wearer's torso and head remain out of view behind the camera throughout all five frames. Compared to the blurry RGB image in frame 3, the pose map clearly resolves the exact joint articulation and orientation of the wearer's five fingers relative to the wrist. However, the pose map is unreliable in frame 4, where it completely fails to detect both the camera wearer's left hand on the lower left and right hand on the lower right (each about 0.4 to 0.6 metres from the camera and touching the dog's ears and toy), partly due to motion blur and partial occlusion by the dog's floppy ears.
